fight: Can a software factory run 100+ worker agents with minimal human review and expect production-grade reliability, or does current evidence show agent autonomy at that scale requires heavy governance scaffolding before it is safe?

side_a.position: Vertically-integrated, in-house multi-agent infrastructure accelerates delivery and parallel multi-agent software construction at scale is feasible today, justifying ambitious concurrency targets.
claims: Sierra built its own Kubernetes-native agent sandbox orchestration layer (Agency) because the agent-sandbox problem space was too undefined to inherit someone else's trade-offs; vertically-integrated infra accelerates feature delivery.
Feasibility of parallel multi-agent software construction at scale (Berkeley RDI).

side_b.position: Frontier agents are not yet reliably autonomous across long-horizon software maintenance; blast radius from excess permissions can be catastrophic and near-instantaneous, architectural drift is self-reinforcing across sessions absent governance, and existing security/review tooling is insufficient to audit agent-generated code at this scale.
claims: Refutes claim that frontier agents are already reliably autonomous across long-horizon software maintenance tasks (Berkeley RDI).

Agent blast radius can be catastrophic and near-instantaneous when permissions exceed task scope; AI-generated architectural drift is self-reinforcing across successive agent sessions absent hard constraints; existing security tooling is insufficient for auditing agent-generated code (Shipped by Agents).
LLM code-understanding quality is not uniform; direct LLM code translation cannot be trusted for critical modules (legacy modernization survey).
Human oversight moves up a level rather than disappearing in a layered QC architecture (The New Stack).

evidence_quality_delta: Side B is stronger: empirical production-incident framing (Shipped by Agents), a peer-reviewed-adjacent survey on LLM code-understanding limits, and an academic autonomy-levels framework (Berkeley) that explicitly refutes the strong claim. Side A's feasibility claims are real but narrower in scope (infra capability, not reliability-at-scale) — the same Berkeley source straddles both sides, which is itself evidence the fight is genuine rather than manufactured.
scope_overlap: Partially scoped differently: Side A argues capability/feasibility of building the infrastructure; Side B argues reliability/safety of operating it with reduced human oversight. Both can be true simultaneously — the resolution is that scale is achievable but only with the governance layer Side B demands, which is exactly the architectural answer this report must give.

fight: Do Agent Skills (SOPs-as-callable-capabilities) reduce operating cost and context overhead as vendor guidance claims, or does empirical measurement show real, non-negligible token overhead that complicates the cost-optimization pillar?

side_a.position: Encoding SOPs as Agent Skills with progressive disclosure reduces context overhead and token spend versus loading full procedural instructions inline; deterministic Skill sequences improve reliability at lower cost.
claims: SOPs encoded as Agent Skills reduce context overhead at scale (Claude platform docs).
Deterministic code execution via Skills reduces token spend versus naive prompting (Claude platform docs).
Converting SOPs into deterministic Agent Skill sequences improves reliability (addyosmani agent-skills performance-optimization SKILL.md).

side_b.position: Measured independently, Skill-body loading carries a real, quantified token overhead; adding rules to Skills is not free, and progressive disclosure does not fully neutralize that cost — Skill content measurably changes agent behavior and Skill size directly trades off against runtime context budget.
claims: Refutes that progressive disclosure (Anthropic's recommended context-isolation pattern) eliminates overhead.
Refutes that adding rules to Skills is free; a meaningful fraction of the context budget is consumed.
Skill size directly trades off against runtime context budget (agent-skill-evolution empirical study).

evidence_quality_delta: Side B is a single source but it is the only one in the corpus doing direct empirical measurement (quantified token overhead, reproducible effect of Skill content on behavior) versus Side A's vendor-documentation framing. Empirical-single-source still outranks documentation-framing-multiple-source on this specific numeric question.
scope_overlap: Genuine disagreement on magnitude, not direction — both sides agree Skills are net-useful; they disagree on whether the overhead is negligible (vendor framing) or material enough to budget for explicitly (empirical study). The report should present Skills as a net win while explicitly budgeting for their non-zero context cost, rather than treating them as free.
